title: Islam: begin with mercy
hook: almost every chapter opens: in the name of God, most gracious, most merciful (Quran 1:1)

segments.voice: Yesterday: dhikr, remembrance, one word said again and again. Your line was hearts find rest. Did your word carry you anywhere? Day two hundred seventy.

Think about how you start things. An email: per my last message. A hard conversation: we need to talk. A Monday: with a groan. The first words set the weather for everything after them. Now open a Qur'an. Turn to almost any chapter, one hundred thirteen of its one hundred fourteen, and before anything else, before law or story or warning, you'll find the same opening line. It names God, and then, twice over, it names mercy. Today, on our visit to Islam: Rahman, and the habit of beginning with mercy.
screen: `PER MY LAST MESSAGE.` → `THE SAME FIRST LINE, 113 TIMES.` → `MERCY, TWICE OVER.`

segments.voice: The line is called the basmala, and it opens the very first chapter. In Marmaduke Pickthall's 1930 translation: "In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful." In Arabic: bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim. Two names for God, and both grow from the same three-letter root, r-h-m. Rahman is the vast, overflowing mercy that covers everything and everyone. Rahim is the steady, caring mercy that stays close. Scholars have written whole books on the difference. And here is what surprises people: in Arabic, the same root gives the word rahim, the womb. A hadith reports God saying: I am ar-Rahman; I created the womb and gave it a name drawn from my own. Mercy, in this language, is the love of a mother for the child she carries. Another hadith, in Sahih al-Bukhari, says that when God created the world, God wrote: my mercy prevails over my wrath. And another, that God divided mercy into a hundred parts and sent just one down to earth; from that single part, a mother animal lifts her hoof so as not to hurt her young. Only one chapter, the ninth, doesn't open with the basmala, and scholars give different reasons. But the line appears again inside chapter twenty-seven, in a letter from Solomon, so the count comes out at one hundred fourteen. Muslims say bismillah before eating, driving, starting work, even entering a room. Beginning with God's name is beginning with mercy, and many Muslims say it sets the weather for what follows.
screen: `THE BASMALA OPENS THE BOOK.` · `RAHMAN AND RAHIM: ONE ROOT.` · `RAHIM — THE WOMB.` · `MY MERCY PREVAILS OVER MY WRATH.` · then, large: `BEGIN WITH MERCY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: begin one task with a kind word. Sit, and think of the next thing you'll start: a message, a meeting, a chore, a conversation with someone difficult. Picture its first words. Now soften them. Replace per my last message with thanks for this. Replace we need to talk with I've been thinking about you. If you pray, you might begin with bismillah. The bell holds the time.
Rahman. The Most Merciful: mercy that overflows, from the same root as the word for womb, named at the start of almost every chapter. Today's word.
Your line: begin with mercy. Today, open your next hard message or conversation with one kind sentence, and see how the weather changes. Day two hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Muslims recite the basmala at the start of each chapter of the Qur'an and say bismillah before eating, traveling, working and many ordinary acts.

pairs: the line that opens the chapters

myth: every chapter of the Qur'an opens with the basmala
113 of 114 do; the ninth doesn't, though the line appears inside chapter 27.
Rahman and the Arabic word for womb share a root
r-h-m: mercy as a mother's love.
a hadith says God's mercy prevails over God's wrath

fork.setup: a hadith says God divided mercy into a hundred parts. how many were sent down to earth?
fork.reveal: just one part, the hadith says; from it, even a mother animal lifts her hoof so as not to hurt her young.

original.note: Arabic: the Most Merciful, from the root r-h-m.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Muslim name, like Abdul Rahman.
what it means: the Most Merciful, God's overflowing mercy, named at the start of almost every chapter.
what a scholar hears: Rahman and Rahim share r-h-m with rahim, womb; surah 9 lacks the basmala and 27:30 contains it, so it occurs 114 times.

sources.quoted: In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful.

sources.ref: Sunan Abi Dawud 1694 (the womb and the name ar-Rahman)

notes: Hadith references: 'my mercy prevails over my wrath' (Bukhari 3194), mercy in a hundred parts (Bukhari 6000), the womb named from ar-Rahman (Abu Dawud 1694; also Tirmidhi 1907). Confirm numbering and paraphrases.
Distinction between Rahman and Rahim is a common scholarly reading, not the only one.
Surah 9 without the basmala: several explanations exist; the script says so without choosing.
